basic_information.name: International Network of AI Safety Institutes (AISI Network)
basic_information.jurisdiction: Global — initial members: Australia, Canada, EU, France, Japan, Kenya, Republic of Korea, Singapore, United Kingdom, United States
basic_information.effective_date: Seoul Statement of Intent signed 21 May 2024 (AI Seoul Summit); inaugural convening 20-21 November 2024 in San Francisco; joint findings presented at Paris AI Action Summit 10-11 February 2025

scope_and_content.summary: A multilateral network of government-backed AI safety institutes and offices whose mission is to promote the safe, secure, and trustworthy development of AI. Born from the Bletchley Park AI Safety Summit (November 2023) and formalised via the Seoul Statement of Intent (May 2024), the Network coordinates international research on frontier AI risks, joint model testing, and shared safety standards. It brings together 10 member entities (as of February 2025) and operates on a voluntary, technically-focused basis rather than imposing binding legal obligations.
key_provisions: Joint mission statement committing members to advance the science of AI safety through international coordination based on openness, transparency, and reciprocity
Three priority work areas: (1) managing risks from synthetic content, (2) testing foundation models, and (3) conducting risk assessments for advanced AI systems

Multilateral model testing exercises — first exercise results shared at the San Francisco convening (Nov 2024), second exercise led by Singapore, Japan, and UK presented at Paris AI Action Summit (Feb 2025)

Over $11 million in global research funding committed toward synthetic content research, including $3.8M from USAID, $3M from Knight Foundation, $1M from AI Safety Fund, $250K from Omidyar Network, and $7.2M from South Korea (over 4 years)
Joint statement on risk assessments of advanced AI systems
Sharing of information about models including capabilities, limitations, and risks; exchange or joint creation of evaluations, datasets, and associated criteria
Promotion of international standards development and appropriate research security practices
Open engagement commitment — actively engaging countries, partners, and stakeholders in all regions and at all levels of development
Open-sourcing of safety tools — UK AISI released 'Inspect' (AI model evaluation tool) as open source in May 2024
Research agenda encouraging multidisciplinary approaches including technical mitigations and social scientific/humanistic assessments
scope_and_content.risk_classification: The Network itself does not impose a risk classification system. However, its work on risk assessments for advanced AI systems contributes to building common frameworks for evaluating frontier model risks across jurisdictions. Individual member institutes apply their own national risk frameworks (e.g., EU AI Act risk tiers, UK's sector-specific approach). The Network's joint testing exercises aim to develop interoperable evaluation methodologies.
scope_and_content.covered_entities: The Network is an intergovernmental coordination mechanism. It directly engages government AI safety institutes and offices from member countries. Indirectly, its standards, evaluations, and best practices affect AI developers (especially frontier model developers), deployers, and the research community. The US AISI consortium alone includes 200+ companies and organizations.
scope_and_content.sector_scope: Cross-sector — focused on frontier/general-purpose AI models rather than sector-specific applications. Priority domains include synthetic content (deepfakes, misinformation), foundation model safety, and advanced AI risk assessment. No sectors are explicitly exempted, though the primary focus is on the most capable AI systems.
scope_and_content.open_source_treatment: The Network actively promotes open-source safety tools. The UK AISI open-sourced 'Inspect', an AI safety evaluation framework, in May 2024. The Network's research agenda and evaluation methodologies are intended to be shared publicly. There is no restriction or special treatment for open-source AI models within the Network's framework — it focuses on evaluating capabilities and risks regardless of licensing model.
scope_and_content.extraterritorial_reach: As a voluntary international agreement, the Network has no formal extraterritorial legal reach. However, its practical influence extends globally through: (1) harmonised safety standards that may become de facto requirements for frontier AI developers seeking multi-market access; (2) shared evaluation results that inform national regulatory decisions; (3) the participation of major AI-producing nations (US, UK, EU, Japan, Korea) whose combined market power creates strong incentive for compliance; (4) the US CAISI explicitly stated its role includes 'representing American interests internationally, guarding against burdensome regulation of US technologies by foreign governments'.

compliance_and_enforcement.penalties: None — the Network operates on a purely voluntary basis. It produces guidelines, best practices, shared research, and joint evaluation findings but has no enforcement mechanism or penalty structure. Enforcement remains at the national level through each member's domestic regulatory framework.
compliance_and_enforcement.enforcement_body: No centralised enforcement body. The US served as inaugural chair of the Network (through the US AISI, now CAISI within NIST). Coordination functions include aligning research agendas, facilitating working groups, standardising evaluations, organising meetings and events, and representing the Network internationally. Each member institute operates under its own national authority: UK AISI (now AI Security Institute) under DSIT, US AISI (now CAISI) under NIST/Commerce, Japan AISI under METI, EU AI Office under European Commission DG Connect, etc.
compliance_and_enforcement.compliance_timeline: Key milestones: Nov 2023 — UK AISI established at Bletchley Park Summit, US AISI announced within NIST; Feb 2024 — Japan AISI launched; May 2024 — Seoul Statement of Intent signed, Network concept formalised; Nov 2024 — inaugural convening in San Francisco, mission statement adopted, first joint testing results; Feb 2025 — second joint testing exercise results presented at Paris AI Action Summit; Jul 2025 — third directors-level meeting in Vancouver; Feb 2026 — AI Impact Summit in New Delhi (next major multilateral AI summit). Ongoing: regular directors-level meetings, working group sessions on priority topics.
compliance_and_enforcement.reporting_requirements: No mandatory reporting. Members voluntarily share: (1) findings from domestic AI evaluations; (2) results of joint multilateral testing exercises; (3) research outputs on synthetic content, model testing, and risk assessment; (4) progress updates at international summits. The Network committed to producing joint publications including the International AI Safety Report (first edition published February 2025, involving 96 experts; 2026 update expected early 2026).
compliance_and_enforcement.sme_provisions: No specific SME provisions within the Network framework itself. However, the Network's work on shared evaluation standards and open-source safety tools (like Inspect) indirectly benefits SMEs by reducing the cost of safety evaluation. Individual member institutes may have SME-specific programs — e.g., the US AISI consortium includes startups, and EU regulatory sandboxes offer SME priority access.

impact_and_analysis.business_impact: LARGE ENTERPRISES (frontier AI labs): Directly affected through voluntary engagement with national AISIs for pre-deployment testing — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta, and others have signed agreements with the UK and US AISIs for pre-release model access. These agreements are voluntary but create industry norms that may become harder to avoid. STARTUPS AND SMEs: Indirect impact — the Network's harmonised evaluation standards could reduce the compliance fragmentation problem (currently estimated at $160K-$330K per jurisdiction for high-risk AI). If the Network succeeds in creating interoperable standards, a single evaluation could satisfy multiple jurisdictions, reducing market access costs. However, if standards diverge (as signalled by US/UK rebranding away from 'safety'), startups may face competing frameworks. COMPLIANCE MARKET: The Network creates demand for AI safety evaluation tools, testing services, and risk assessment expertise — a growing market opportunity. COMPETITIVE DYNAMICS: Companies that voluntarily participate in AISI evaluations may gain a trust premium; those that don't may face reputational risk in safety-conscious markets (EU, healthcare, finance).
impact_and_analysis.innovation_effect: Primarily intended to promote innovation by reducing uncertainty. PROMOTING factors: (1) shared evaluation standards reduce duplication — one well-designed test accepted across 10 jurisdictions is more efficient than 10 different national tests; (2) open-source safety tools (Inspect) lower barriers to safety evaluation; (3) multilateral testing exercises build collective knowledge about frontier AI capabilities and risks; (4) the Network's voluntary nature avoids the compliance burden of hard regulation. CONSTRAINING concerns: (1) divergence between US/UK 'innovation-first' rebranding and EU/others' safety-first approach may fragment the Network's effectiveness; (2) voluntary commitments may not be sufficient for genuinely dangerous AI capabilities; (3) if Network standards eventually become de facto mandatory (through incorporation into national regulations), they could constrain innovation without the democratic legitimacy of legislation.
impact_and_analysis.global_influence: Significant as the first multilateral technical cooperation mechanism specifically for AI safety. The Network creates a potential foundation for future international AI governance — analogous to early nuclear safety cooperation that led to the IAEA. The inclusion of Kenya and Singapore alongside G7 nations signals Global South engagement. However, notable absences include China, India, and most developing nations. The Network's influence is being tested by: (1) the US rebranding from 'safety' to 'standards and innovation', signalling reduced commitment to safety-focused cooperation under the Trump administration; (2) the UK's parallel shift from 'safety' to 'security'; (3) the 2026 New Delhi AI Impact Summit representing a shift of multilateral AI governance toward the Global South. The 'Bletchley-Seoul-Paris-New Delhi' summit sequence is establishing a regular cadence for international AI governance.
impact_and_analysis.stakeholder_positions: SUPPORTIVE: Most G7 governments (at least initially), EU AI Office, civil society organisations focused on AI safety (Future of Life Institute, Center for AI Safety, All Tech Is Human), academia (International AI Safety Report involved 96 experts). The technology industry has generally engaged cooperatively — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta signed voluntary pre-deployment testing agreements. CRITICAL/CONCERNED: (1) Elizabeth Seger (Demos) and Michael Birtwistle (Ada Lovelace Institute) criticised the UK/US rebranding for abandoning bias and broader safety concerns; (2) AI Now Institute warned the UK rebranding represents a 'sharp turn' away from meaningful safety oversight; (3) European Policy Centre argued Paris Summit marked 'Au Revoir to global AI Safety' as focus shifted to innovation; (4) Global South critics note the Network is dominated by wealthy nations despite AI risks affecting all countries; (5) Trump administration explicitly framed the US rebranding as rejecting 'censorship and regulations under the guise of national security' (Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick).
impact_and_analysis.deregulatory_signals: Yes, strong deregulatory signals from the two founding members. US: In June 2025, the Trump administration rebranded the US AISI as the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), explicitly dropping 'safety' from the name and mission. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stated: 'Innovators will no longer be limited by these standards.' CAISI's stated role shifted to facilitating voluntary industry engagement and guarding against foreign regulation of US technologies. UK: In February 2025, the UK AISI was renamed the AI Security Institute, narrowing focus to national security threats and explicitly excluding bias and freedom of speech from its scope. These rebranding signals have not formally dissolved the Network, but they fundamentally alter the balance between safety and innovation within the two most influential member institutes. Other members (EU, Japan, Korea, Singapore) have not signalled similar deregulatory shifts.

related_regulations: Bletchley Declaration (November 2023) — foundational agreement from the first AI Safety Summit, signed by 28 countries, establishing the need for international AI safety cooperation
Seoul Declaration for Safe, Innovative and Inclusive AI (May 2024) — political declaration by leaders at AI Seoul Summit committing to AI safety and the AISI Network
Seoul Statement of Intent toward International Cooperation on AI Safety Science (May 2024) — the specific annex establishing the Network's mandate and cooperation framework
Paris AI Action Summit Statement (February 2025) — follow-on multilateral declaration on inclusive and sustainable AI
EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) — the EU's comprehensive AI regulation; EU AI Office participates in the Network
US Executive Order 14110 on AI (October 2023) — Biden-era order that established the US AISI; rescinded by Trump EO 14179 (January 2025)
Trump Executive Order 14179 on AI (January 2025) — replaced Biden AI order, reoriented US AI policy toward innovation
Frontier AI Safety Commitments (Seoul, May 2024) — voluntary commitments by leading AI companies on safety practices
International AI Safety Report (February 2025, updated 2026) — scientific report produced by 96 experts, endorsed at Paris Summit
OECD AI Principles — broader international framework for responsible AI that the Network's work complements
key_actors: US Department of Commerce / NIST — hosts the US AISI (now CAISI), served as inaugural Network chair. Secretary Howard Lutnick led the 2025 rebranding
UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) — hosts the UK AISI (now AI Security Institute), originally established by PM Rishi Sunak
Gina Raimondo — former US Commerce Secretary (Biden admin), led the Network's launch at the San Francisco convening in November 2024
Japan Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) — hosts the Japan AISI, launched February 2024
European Commission / EU AI Office — EU member of the Network, led by Director Lucilla Sioli
France — Inria and LNE partnership for AI evaluation; hosted the Paris AI Action Summit (Feb 2025)
Korea AISI — established November 2024, South Korea pledged $7.2M for synthetic content research
Singapore — active participant, co-led the second joint testing exercise with Japan and UK
Canada — Canadian AI Safety Institute (CAISI) participates; hosted third directors-level meeting in Vancouver (July 2025)
Kenya — first African member, though formal AISI establishment status is unclear
Australia — participates in directors-level meetings; AISI establishment ongoing
Knight Foundation, USAID, AI Safety Fund, Omidyar Network — major funders of Network research
Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta — frontier AI companies with voluntary pre-deployment testing agreements with member AISIs
recent_developments: Nov 2024: Inaugural convening in San Francisco — mission statement adopted, $11M+ in research funding announced, first multilateral testing exercise results shared, joint risk assessment statement released

Feb 2025: Paris AI Action Summit — Network presented second joint testing exercise results (led by Singapore, Japan, UK); International AI Safety Report published (96 experts); UK AISI renamed to AI Security Institute, narrowing scope to security threats
Jan 2025: Trump Executive Order 14179 rescinded Biden's AI EO 14110, signalling US policy shift toward deregulation
Jun 2025: US AISI rebranded as Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), dropping 'safety' from name and mission; Commerce Secretary Lutnick frames shift as anti-censorship, pro-innovation
Jul 2025: Third directors-level meeting held in Vancouver, Canada; Australia confirmed attendance
Oct 2025: International AI Safety Report updated with major breakthroughs section on AI capabilities
Jan 2026: CAISI issued Request for Information on security considerations for AI agents, signalling continued technical engagement despite rebranding
Feb 2026: Next major milestone — AI Impact Summit in New Delhi (first multilateral AI summit hosted in Global South); 2026 International AI Safety Report update expected
Ongoing: Network continues operations despite US/UK rebranding; consortium of 200+ organizations within US CAISI reportedly still operational but future uncertain

teaching_relevance.entrepreneurial_implications: HIGH RELEVANCE for AI entrepreneurs navigating the emerging international safety landscape. KEY IMPLICATIONS: (1) STANDARDS CONVERGENCE vs FRAGMENTATION — if the Network succeeds in harmonising evaluation standards across 10 jurisdictions, startups benefit from 'test once, deploy everywhere'; if it fragments (as signalled by US/UK rebranding), startups face expensive multi-jurisdiction compliance. Entrepreneurs should monitor whether Network standards achieve de facto acceptance. (2) VOLUNTARY PRE-DEPLOYMENT TESTING — frontier AI companies are voluntarily sharing models with AISIs for pre-release testing; startups building on these models benefit from upstream safety validation, reducing their own compliance burden. (3) OPEN-SOURCE SAFETY TOOLS — the Network's open-source tools (UK Inspect framework) lower the cost of safety evaluation for startups that cannot afford proprietary testing infrastructure. (4) TRUST PREMIUM — startups that can demonstrate alignment with internationally recognised safety standards gain credibility with enterprise customers, investors, and regulators; this is especially valuable in regulated sectors (healthcare, finance, public sector). (5) GEOPOLITICAL RISK — the US/UK rebranding away from 'safety' toward 'innovation/security' creates uncertainty about the Network's future direction; European entrepreneurs should prepare for a scenario where EU safety standards diverge from US/UK approaches, creating distinct market requirements. (6) MARKET OPPORTUNITY — AI safety evaluation, testing, and compliance tools represent a growing market as the Network's standards potentially become baseline expectations. (7) SYNTHETIC CONTENT — the Network's $11M+ research investment in synthetic content safety creates both constraints (on deepfake-generating tools) and opportunities (for detection/watermarking startups).
teaching_relevance.session_mapping: Session 5 (Ethics, governance & final presentations) — primary session for understanding international AI safety cooperation and its geopolitical dynamics. Also relevant to Session 1 (Fundamentals & AI landscape) for understanding the global AI governance ecosystem, and Session 3 (Framing & managing AI projects) for understanding how international safety standards affect project planning and market access decisions.

confidence.data_quality: High — based on official government sources (NIST fact sheet, UK GOV.UK publications, Canadian ISED mission statement, European Commission digital strategy pages), established policy think tanks (CSIS, Atlantic Council, European Policy Centre, All Tech Is Human, IAPS), and major news outlets (TIME, NBC News, FedScoop, CIO Dive). The Network's formation timeline is well-documented across multiple independent sources.
confidence.cross_reference: NIST (nist.gov), UK Government (gov.uk), Canadian Government (ised-isde.canada.ca), European Commission (digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu), CSIS, ANSI, SIIA, Atlantic Council, European Policy Centre, Future of Life Institute, Centre for Future Generations, OECD AI Observatory, All Tech Is Human, AI Now Institute, Wikipedia (AI Safety Institute). Funding figures cross-referenced between NIST fact sheet and ANSI report.
confidence.caveats: The Network's status is highly uncertain as of early 2026: (1) The two founding and most influential members (US, UK) have both rebranded their institutes away from 'safety', raising questions about the Network's continued coherence and direction; (2) The US AISI consortium of 200+ organizations may be wound down under the Trump administration; (3) The 'voluntary' nature means members can disengage without consequence; (4) China and India — two of the world's largest AI developers — are not members; (5) The Network has no permanent secretariat, formal legal status, or guaranteed funding beyond specific research commitments; (6) The shift from 'safety' to 'security/innovation' in the US and UK may reduce the Network's focus on broader societal risks (bias, fairness, environmental impact) in favour of narrow national security concerns; (7) The New Delhi AI Impact Summit (Feb 2026) may reshape the Network's direction as Global South voices gain influence.
